_readme: This file is the content source for every case study on the site.
Add, edit or delete a project here, run `node build.js`, and the work/ pages,
the portfolio grid and the home-page rail all follow. Nothing else to touch.
Required on every project: slug, service, client, industry, headline,
statement, card. Everything else is optional — a section whose data is
missing is dropped from the page rather than rendered empty.
WARNING: every client, quote and number below is invented placeholder copy.
See CONTENT-TO-REPLACE.md. None of it should survive a public launch.

projects.headline: Enquiries up 3.2× in 90 days
projects.statement: Rebuilding a jewellery brand’s site around the enquiry rather than the catalogue, so showroom-quality conversations start online.

card.blurb: A conversion-led rebuild that put the enquiry path on every page, not just the contact form.
card.quote: The new site does the selling our showroom used to do.

hero.label: Homepage — desktop
hero.caption: The rebuilt homepage leads with the consultation, not the carousel.

challenge.title: A catalogue that stopped short of the conversation
challenge.lead: Aarna sells pieces that people want to see, hold and ask about before buying. The old site behaved like a lookbook: it showed the range beautifully and then left visitors with a single contact form buried in the footer.
points: Product pages ended at a price and a photograph. There was no way to ask about resizing, stone substitution or a custom commission — the three questions that start almost every sale.
Mobile traffic was the majority of sessions and the minority of enquiries. The form was the narrowest part of the funnel and it was also the hardest thing to fill in on a phone.
challenge.objective: Turn browsing into a booked consultation without turning the brand into a discount store.

strategy.title: Design the enquiry, then design around it
strategy.lead: We treated the enquiry as the product. Every template was then judged on one question: does this page make the next conversation easier to start?
principles: Put a contextual enquiry on every product page
Lead with craft and provenance, not price
Collapse the journey to three steps on mobile
Make custom commissions a visible path, not a footnote

decisions.title: An enquiry form that already knows the piece
decisions.body: Each product page carries its own enquiry panel, pre-filled with the piece, the metal and the size being viewed. The visitor adds a question and a phone number; nothing else is asked.
decisions.why: The old form asked people to describe what they were looking at. Pre-filling removed the step most likely to lose a mobile visitor mid-thought, and gave the sales team a qualified brief instead of a name and an email address.

decisions.title: Custom commissions given their own journey
decisions.body: Bespoke work moved out of a paragraph on the About page into a dedicated path with its own gallery, timeline and starting price band.
decisions.why: Commissions are the highest-value work and the hardest to explain. Showing the process and the honest timeline up front attracted better-matched enquiries and filtered out the ones that were never going to convert.

decisions.title: Craft shown before the price
decisions.body: Product templates open with material, origin and making detail. Price sits below the fold, next to the enquiry, rather than competing with the first photograph.
decisions.why: Buyers at this price point decide on trust first. Leading with provenance gave the price somewhere to land.

designSystem.title: A small system the team can actually run
designSystem.lead: Enough structure to keep 200 product pages consistent, and no more than the in-house team could maintain without a designer on call.

items.v: Two weights, one display face, a fixed six-step scale
Warm neutral base, single accent reserved for enquiry actions
14 reusable sections, each with a mobile rule
Fixed crop ratios so new product shots drop in without reflowing

implementation.title: Built as sections, not as pages
implementation.lead: The approved design shipped as a responsive Shopify theme assembled from reusable sections, so the team can build a new landing page without needing a developer or a redesign.
points: 14 section types, each configurable from the Shopify editor
Enquiry submissions routed to the sales inbox and to the CRM
Product imagery served responsively; largest contentful paint under 2s on 4G
Collection and campaign pages composable from the same sections

projects.resultsNote: Measured over the 90 days after launch against the 90 days before, same traffic sources.
projects.takeaway: Treating the enquiry as the product — rather than as the thing that happens after the product — turned a catalogue into a source of qualified conversations, without discounting or widening the range.

projects.headline: Organic enquiries up 4.1× in eight months
projects.statement: Rebuilding an interiors studio’s service pages around what buyers actually search for, then earning the links to rank them.

card.blurb: Rebuilt the service pages around what buyers actually search for, then earned the links to rank them.
card.quote: We stopped buying every lead. Search does that for us now.

hero.label: Organic sessions — 12-month trend
hero.caption: Non-brand organic sessions, month on month.

challenge.title: Ranking for the studio’s name and nothing else
challenge.lead: Northline had a decade of completed projects and a site that search engines read as a single page about a company. Almost all organic traffic was people who already knew the name.
symptoms: One thin page covered every service, from full-home interiors to modular kitchens
Project pages carried no text, so the portfolio was invisible to search
Competitors with weaker work outranked them on every commercial query
Paid search was covering the gap at a cost that rose every quarter

strategy.title: Match the page to the question
strategy.lead: Buyers search by service, by room and by city, in that order. The site had none of those pages. Our approach was to build the missing layer, prove it with real projects, then earn the links that make it rank.

pillars.title: Search intent
pillars.body: We separated research queries from hiring queries. Research got guides; hiring got service pages with pricing bands, timelines and a brief form.

pillars.title: Keyword priority
pillars.body: Queries were ranked on business value first and volume second, so a low-volume query for full-home interiors outranked a high-volume one about colour trends.

pillars.title: Technical base
pillars.body: Fixed indexation of the project archive, cut render-blocking assets, and gave every project a crawlable URL with real copy.

pillars.title: Internal linking
pillars.body: Every project page now links up to the service it belongs to and across to the city page, so authority collects where the enquiries are.

changes.title: Technical SEO
changes.body: Resolved the duplicate-URL pattern that had the project archive indexed four ways, cut unused scripts, and brought median mobile load from 4.6s to 1.9s.

changes.title: On-page SEO
changes.body: Rewrote titles, headings and metadata across 60 pages so each one answers a single query rather than describing the company.

changes.title: Content
changes.body: Built nine service pages and six city pages, each carrying real project photography, a cost band and a brief form.

changes.title: Site structure
changes.body: Connected 120 project pages to the services and cities they belong to, turning an orphaned portfolio into the site’s strongest internal-link asset.

projects.growthNote: Search Console and GA4, eight-month campaign window against the eight months preceding it.

impact.title: The same pipeline, at a lower cost of acquisition
impact.lead: Organic went from a trickle of brand searches to the studio’s largest source of qualified enquiries.
points: Because the new pages carry a cost band and a brief form, the enquiries arriving through search are better qualified than the paid ones they replaced — the sales team reports fewer first calls that end in a budget mismatch.
Paid search spend was reduced by roughly a third over the campaign without a fall in total enquiries, which is where most of the commercial benefit sits.

projects.takeaway: A portfolio is only an SEO asset once it is connected to the pages people actually search for. Building that missing layer — and linking the existing work into it — did more than any amount of new content would have.

projects.headline: ROAS held at 4.6× on a doubled budget
projects.statement: Fixing attribution first for a growing wellness brand, then scaling only the campaigns the numbers could defend.

card.blurb: Fixed attribution first, then scaled only the campaigns the numbers could defend.
card.quote: The first month, we finally knew which ads paid.

hero.label: Blended ROAS — weekly
hero.caption: Blended return on ad spend against weekly budget.

challenge.title: Spending more without knowing what worked
challenge.lead: Veda was spending steadily across two platforms and could not say which half was working. Platform-reported conversions added up to roughly twice the orders the business actually took.
symptoms: Meta and Google both claimed the same purchases, so neither number could be trusted
Budget was split evenly out of caution rather than evidence
One subscription product carried most of the margin and none of the spend
Creative had not been refreshed in five months and frequency was climbing

campaign.title: Fix the measurement, then let it decide the budget
campaign.lead: Nothing was scaled in the first three weeks. We rebuilt tracking until platform numbers reconciled with the order table, and only then started moving money.
campaign.audience: Repeat-purchase-likely buyers aged 28–45, split into first-order and subscription-intent segments
campaign.offer: First-order discount retired in favour of a subscription trial with free shipping
campaign.creative: Founder-led video and ingredient-provenance stills, refreshed fortnightly

funnel.body: Segment-matched creative, with the subscription offer shown only to subscription-intent audiences.
A page per product rather than the homepage, with the ad’s claim repeated above the fold.
One-step cart with the subscription option pre-selected for the matching segment.
Purchase confirmed server-side, deduplicated against the order table before it reaches either platform.

execution.title: Campaign structure
execution.body: Collapsed 31 overlapping ad sets into six, split by intent rather than by product, so the platforms stopped bidding against themselves.

execution.title: Creative
execution.body: Three concepts in rotation at any time, each with a founder-led and a product-led cut, refreshed on a fortnightly cycle.

execution.title: Landing pages
execution.body: Replaced the homepage destination with a page per product, each echoing the specific claim the ad made.

execution.title: Measurement
execution.body: Server-side events with order-ID deduplication, so a purchase is counted once regardless of how many platforms claim it.

optimisations.decision: Retired the broad prospecting audience on Meta
optimisations.reason: It carried 38% of spend and, once deduplicated, almost none of the first-time orders.
optimisations.outcome: Budget moved to intent segments; cost per acquisition fell in the following fortnight.

optimisations.decision: Moved the subscription offer ahead of the discount
optimisations.reason: First-order discounting was buying one-time buyers at close to break-even.
optimisations.outcome: Lower first-order volume, materially higher contribution per customer.

optimisations.decision: Shifted Shopping budget to the four highest-margin SKUs
optimisations.reason: Spend had been distributed across the full catalogue regardless of margin.
optimisations.outcome: Same revenue on lower spend, which is most of the ROAS improvement.

optimisations.decision: Set a fortnightly creative refresh
optimisations.reason: Frequency crossed 3.4 before performance visibly dropped, so decay was predictable.
optimisations.outcome: Click-through rate stabilised instead of sagging between refreshes.

projects.beforeAfterNote: Month five against month zero. Both periods use the same deduplicated server-side measurement, so the “before” figures are restated rather than taken from the original platform reports.

businessResult.title: Budget doubled, return held
businessResult.lead: The point of the work was not a higher ROAS at the same spend — it was a defensible ROAS at a spend the business could keep increasing.
points: Monthly spend went from ₹4.2L to ₹8.6L while blended return rose, which is the combination that lets a D2C brand plan inventory rather than react to it.
Subscription-first acquisition raised contribution per customer, so the same ROAS now represents more margin than it did at the start.

projects.takeaway: Measurement was the campaign. Once the platforms stopped double-counting, the budget decisions made themselves — and the brand could spend twice as much with more confidence than it had at half the spend.

projects.headline: Project enquiries up 2.4× after launch
projects.statement: A quieter site for an architecture practice that lets the work make the argument, with a brief form that filters badly matched leads.

card.blurb: A quieter site that lets the work make the argument, with a brief form that filters badly matched leads.
card.quote: Clients arrive already understanding how we work.

hero.label: Project page — desktop
hero.caption: Full-bleed project photography with the drawing set alongside.

challenge.title: Good work, badly matched enquiries
challenge.lead: Studio Mehr was not short of enquiries. It was short of the right ones. Most first calls ended on budget or scope, which cost the practice several hours a week and told prospective clients nothing before they picked up the phone.
points: The site showed finished photography and almost nothing about process, fees or how a project runs.
The contact form asked for a name and a message, so every enquiry arrived as an unknown quantity.
challenge.objective: Fewer, better-matched enquiries — and a shorter path from first contact to a productive conversation.

strategy.title: Say the hard things earlier
strategy.lead: A practice this size competes on fit, not on volume. The site’s job was to let people disqualify themselves before anyone spent an hour on a call.
principles: Publish the process and the fee structure
Let project pages carry drawings, not just photographs
Replace the contact form with a short brief
Keep the interface quiet so the work stays loud

decisions.title: A brief, not a contact form
decisions.body: The enquiry asks for site location, approximate budget band, timeline and whether planning permission is in place — four questions, each optional, on one screen.
decisions.why: Giving people a budget band to choose from sets expectations without the practice having to name a number first. Enquiries that arrive now carry enough to decide whether a call is worth booking.

decisions.title: Drawings shown next to the photographs
decisions.body: Each project page pairs the finished photography with plans, sections and a short note on what the constraint was.
decisions.why: Clients commissioning architecture are buying judgement. Showing the drawing alongside the result demonstrates it in a way a hero image cannot.

decisions.title: Fees and process made public
decisions.body: A plain page covers stages, what happens in each, roughly how long it takes and how fees are structured.
decisions.why: It removed the single most common reason a first call went nowhere, and it reads as confidence rather than as a price list.

implementation.title: Static where it can be, managed where it must be
implementation.lead: Built as a static site with a headless CMS behind it, so project pages load instantly and the studio can publish a new project without a developer.
points: Projects, drawings and process copy all editable by the studio
Image pipeline generates responsive sets on upload
Brief submissions routed to the principal’s inbox with a structured summary
No analytics beyond first-party page counts, at the practice’s request

projects.takeaway: Publishing the awkward information — fees, timelines, how the practice actually works — reduced the number of enquiries and more than doubled the number worth having.

projects.headline: Non-brand search traffic up 5.8×
projects.statement: Clearing a slow, duplicated catalogue for a speciality food brand, then building the category pages the range deserved.

card.blurb: Cleared a slow, duplicated catalogue, then built the category pages the range deserved.
card.quote: We rank for the things people actually buy.
card.cite: Divya Shah, Growth Lead @ Kesari Foods

hero.label: Indexed pages vs. organic sessions
hero.caption: Index bloat cleared in month two; sessions follow from month three.

challenge.title: Nine thousand pages, four hundred products
challenge.lead: Every filter combination on the catalogue generated a crawlable URL. Google was spending its crawl budget on near-duplicate pages and ranking none of them.
symptoms: 9,100 indexed URLs against roughly 400 real products
Category pages carried no copy, so they competed with each other on identical titles
Median mobile load of 5.2s on the pages that mattered most
Non-brand organic was under 8% of sessions

strategy.title: Remove, then build
strategy.lead: Two phases, deliberately sequential: cut the catalogue down to the pages worth ranking, and only then write the content that would rank them.

pillars.title: Crawl control
pillars.body: Faceted URLs moved behind canonical tags and robots rules, taking the index from 9,100 pages to 640 without losing a single real product.

pillars.title: Category as landing page
pillars.body: Each category became a page about the ingredient — what it is, how it is graded, how to use it — with the products below.

pillars.title: Recipe-led support content
pillars.body: Recipes were built where search demand already existed, each linking into the category it uses rather than sitting in an isolated blog.

pillars.title: Speed
pillars.body: Image pipeline, deferred scripts and a lighter template brought median mobile load from 5.2s to 1.7s.

changes.title: Technical SEO
changes.body: Canonicalised faceted navigation, cleared 8,400 near-duplicate URLs from the index, and fixed the pagination that was orphaning deep catalogue pages.

changes.title: On-page SEO
changes.body: Wrote unique titles, headings and 300–500 words of genuinely useful copy on 38 category pages.

changes.title: Content
changes.body: Published 46 recipes chosen on existing search demand, each linking to the categories it draws from.

changes.title: Site structure
changes.body: Connected recipes, categories and products into clusters, so informational traffic has somewhere commercial to go.

projects.growthNote: Search Console and the store’s own order data, six-month window against the six months preceding it.

impact.title: Organic became the cheapest shelf
impact.lead: Clearing the index did not add traffic by itself. It made the content that followed effective, which is where the growth came from.
points: Recipe traffic now feeds category pages that sell, so informational content earns its place rather than sitting in a blog nobody links to.
Organic revenue overtook paid social in month five, which changed how the brand plans its acquisition mix rather than just its reporting.

projects.takeaway: Most of this campaign was subtraction. The content worked because the crawl budget had somewhere useful to go first.

projects.headline: Cost per booked consult down to ₹640
projects.statement: Tying local campaigns for a dental group to the booking calendar rather than to clicks, with creative refreshed fortnightly.

card.blurb: Local campaigns tied to the booking calendar rather than to clicks, with creative refreshed fortnightly.
card.quote: The chair is full. That is the only metric I check.
card.cite: Dr. Sameer Joshi, Founder @ Lumen Dental

hero.label: Cost per booked consultation — weekly
hero.caption: Cost measured against confirmed calendar bookings, not form fills.

challenge.title: Plenty of leads, empty chairs
challenge.lead: Three clinics were generating form fills at a respectable cost and converting very few of them into attended appointments. The campaigns were optimising for the wrong event.
symptoms: Cost per lead looked healthy; cost per attended consult was never measured
Form fills went to a shared inbox and were followed up when someone had time
All three clinics shared one campaign, so the nearest location was often not the one advertised
Creative ran unchanged for months in a small local audience

campaign.title: Optimise for the calendar, not the form
campaign.lead: We moved the conversion event from form submission to confirmed booking, then let the platforms optimise against the thing the business actually wanted.
campaign.audience: Within 6km of each clinic, split by treatment intent — routine, cosmetic and orthodontic
campaign.offer: Free first consultation with a named clinician and a visible available slot
campaign.creative: Clinician-to-camera video per clinic, refreshed fortnightly

funnel.body: Location-specific creative naming the nearest clinic and the clinician.
One page per clinic, showing live availability rather than a contact form.
Slot picked and confirmed on the page, with an SMS confirmation.
Booking event sent to both platforms, and an attendance event sent the following day.

execution.title: Campaign structure
execution.body: Split one shared campaign into three location campaigns, each with its own radius, budget and landing page.

execution.title: Creative
execution.body: Each clinic’s own clinician on camera, which outperformed the stock-photography set from the first week.

execution.title: Landing pages
execution.body: Replaced the enquiry form with live calendar availability, so the visitor’s next action was booking rather than waiting.

execution.title: Measurement
execution.body: Two conversion events — booking and attendance — so no-shows are visible instead of being counted as success.

optimisations.decision: Moved the optimisation event to confirmed booking
optimisations.reason: Form fills were converting to attended consults at under a third.
optimisations.outcome: Lead volume fell; attended consultations rose in the same fortnight.

optimisations.decision: Split budget by clinic rather than evenly
optimisations.reason: One location had twice the search demand and a third of the budget.
optimisations.outcome: Cost per booking fell fastest at the under-funded clinic.

optimisations.decision: Paused cosmetic keywords during the first month
optimisations.reason: They carried the highest cost and the lowest attendance rate.
optimisations.outcome: Reintroduced in month three with a dedicated page and a realistic price band.

optimisations.decision: Added an SMS reminder 24 hours ahead
optimisations.reason: No-shows were concentrated in bookings made more than four days out.
optimisations.outcome: Attendance rate improved enough to change the effective cost per consult.

projects.beforeAfterNote: Month four against month zero. The “before” cost per booked consult is reconstructed from clinic records, since bookings were not tracked as a conversion at the time.

businessResult.title: A fuller calendar on roughly the same spend
businessResult.lead: Monthly spend rose only marginally. Almost all of the gain came from pointing the same budget at a better-defined outcome.
points: 173 attended consultations a month against 48 is a capacity question rather than a marketing one, which is a better problem for the group to have.
Because attendance is now a tracked event, the clinics can see which treatments and which locations actually fill, and staff accordingly.

projects.takeaway: The campaign did not need more budget or better targeting. It needed to be optimised against the event the business cared about, which turned out to be two steps further down the funnel than anyone was measuring.

projects.headline: Add-to-cart rate up 2.1× on a rebuilt catalogue
projects.statement: Rebuilding a furniture retailer’s product experience around dimensions, materials and delivery — the three things that stop a sale.

card.blurb: Dimensions, materials and delivery windows moved above the fold, where the hesitation actually happens.
card.quote: Returns dropped because people knew what they were buying.
card.cite: Meera Iyer, Head of Retail @ Tamara Living

hero.label: Product page — desktop
hero.caption: Dimensions and delivery window sit alongside the first image.

challenge.title: Beautiful pages that did not answer the question
challenge.lead: Tamara’s product pages opened with a styled room shot and buried the three facts that decide a furniture purchase: will it fit, what is it made of, and when does it arrive.
points: Dimensions sat in a collapsed accordion below four scroll-lengths of photography.
Delivery timing appeared for the first time at checkout, which is where a measurable share of carts were abandoned.
challenge.objective: Let people answer ‘will this work in my room’ without leaving the product page.

strategy.title: Lead with the facts that stop the sale
strategy.lead: Furniture is a considered purchase made against a specific room. The page had to serve that decision before it served the brand.
principles: Dimensions above the fold, always
Delivery window shown before the cart
Material and care stated plainly
Room context as support, not as the headline

decisions.title: A dimensions block beside the first image
decisions.body: Width, depth, height and seat height render as a labelled diagram next to the primary photograph, with a toggle for centimetres and inches.
decisions.why: It answers the first question at the first moment it is asked, instead of sending people to a PDF or a collapsed panel.

decisions.title: Delivery window by pincode, on the product page
decisions.body: A pincode field on the product page returns an estimated delivery window before anything enters the cart.
decisions.why: Delivery surprises at checkout were the largest single cause of abandonment. Moving the answer earlier cost some carts and saved more orders.

designSystem.title: One product template, eleven categories
designSystem.lead: A single configurable template covers everything from a side table to a modular sofa, which is what keeps 600 product pages consistent.

items.v: One face, five steps, tabular figures for all specifications
Neutral base so product photography sets the tone
Dimension diagram, delivery estimator, material card, care panel
Specification blocks reflow to a single column without collapsing into accordions

implementation.title: Shipped on Shopify, specifications driven by metafields
implementation.lead: Every specification is a structured metafield rather than hand-written copy, so the diagram, the filters and the comparison view all read from one source.
points: Dimension diagram generated from metafields, not drawn per product
Delivery estimator backed by the existing logistics API
Bulk import path for the merchandising team
Specification data reused by search filters and the comparison view

projects.takeaway: The photography was never the problem. Moving dimensions and delivery ahead of it turned an attractive catalogue into one people could buy from with confidence.

projects.headline: Course applications up 2.8×
projects.statement: Redesigning an education brand’s digital experience to simplify course discovery and increase applications.

card.blurb: Course discovery became the homepage’s job, instead of a menu item three levels down.
card.quote: Parents find the right course without calling us first.

hero.label: Course finder — desktop
hero.caption: The homepage opens on course discovery rather than on the institute.

challenge.title: A homepage about the institute, not the courses
challenge.lead: Sahana’s 34 courses were reachable only through a dropdown menu three levels deep. The homepage described the institute’s history to an audience that had arrived to compare syllabuses and fees.
points: Prospective students could not filter by format, duration or eligibility without reading every page.
The admissions team spent most of its phone time answering questions the site already contained but did not surface.
challenge.objective: Let a visitor find the right course and start an application in one session.

strategy.title: Make discovery the primary journey
strategy.lead: The homepage was restructured around the information a prospective student needs before choosing a course, rather than treating it as a brand showcase.
principles: Course finder on the homepage
Fees, eligibility and dates on every course page
One application form across all courses
Outcomes shown with the course, not on a separate page

decisions.title: A course finder, not a menu
decisions.body: Visitors filter by field, format, duration and start date, and see matching courses with fees and eligibility on the card itself.
decisions.why: It replaced a navigation problem with a comparison tool, which is what people were trying to do anyway.

decisions.title: Every course page answers the same nine questions
decisions.body: Fees, duration, eligibility, start dates, syllabus, faculty, assessment, outcomes and the application deadline, in that order, on every course.
decisions.why: Consistency makes courses comparable. It also removed most of the repeat questions reaching the admissions desk.

implementation.title: Courses as structured content
implementation.lead: Each course is a structured record rather than a hand-built page, so the finder, the comparison view and the course page all read from the same fields.
points: Custom course type with required fields for fees, dates and eligibility
Finder filters generated from the course data, not maintained separately
One application form, pre-filled with the course being applied to
Admissions team can open and close intakes without editing pages

projects.takeaway: Structuring the courses did more than redesigning the pages. Once every course held the same nine facts, discovery, comparison and application all became straightforward.

projects.headline: Direct sales up 3.4× against the marketplace
projects.statement: Giving an independent publisher a storefront worth buying from directly, instead of sending every reader to a marketplace listing.

card.blurb: A storefront built around the reading sample, so the catalogue stops being a list of covers.
card.quote: We finally own the relationship with our readers.

hero.label: Title page — desktop
hero.caption: Every title opens with a readable sample.

challenge.title: A catalogue that sent its readers elsewhere
challenge.lead: Kavi’s site listed its titles and linked each one to a marketplace. The publisher carried the cost of building an audience and kept neither the margin nor the customer relationship.
points: No sample text, so a reader had no way to judge a book without leaving the site.
Every title page ended in an outbound link, which meant the site had no measurable conversion of its own.
challenge.objective: Make buying directly the obvious choice for a reader who is already on the site.

strategy.title: Sell the writing, not the cover
strategy.lead: Independent publishing competes on taste. The site had to let that taste be experienced rather than described.
principles: A readable sample on every title
Direct purchase as the primary action
Editorial voice carried through the catalogue
Subscriptions for readers who buy on the imprint’s judgement

decisions.title: The first chapter, readable in the page
decisions.body: Every title opens with a properly typeset sample — not a PDF preview — that reads well on a phone.
decisions.why: Readers buy books after reading a few paragraphs. Putting that on the page moved the decision to where the purchase could happen.

decisions.title: A subscription for the imprint, not the title
decisions.body: Readers can subscribe to receive each new release, with the back catalogue at a member price.
decisions.why: It converts people who trust the imprint’s selection into recurring revenue, which is the only reliable income an independent publisher has.

projects.takeaway: Letting readers read was the whole intervention. Everything else on the site existed to get them to the sample and then out of the way.

projects.headline: Online bookings up 4.3× across six locations
projects.statement: Replacing six inconsistent clinic sites with one system that lets patients find the nearest location and book without calling.

card.blurb: One system, six clinics, and a booking flow that works on a phone in a waiting room.
card.quote: Reception answers fewer calls and sees more patients.
card.cite: Dr. Leela Nambiar, Medical Director @ Orva Clinics

hero.label: Location finder — mobile
hero.caption: Nearest clinic, next available slot, two taps.

challenge.title: Six clinics, six websites, one confused patient
challenge.lead: Each Orva location had grown its own site with its own hours, its own services list and its own phone number. Patients routinely arrived at the wrong clinic or called a location that did not offer the service they needed.
points: Opening hours and service lists contradicted each other across locations.
Booking meant calling during business hours, which is exactly when most patients are at work.
challenge.objective: One accurate source of clinic information, and a booking a patient can complete on a phone.

strategy.title: One system, six front doors
strategy.lead: Patients do not think in locations until they need one. The site leads with the service and resolves the location afterwards.
principles: Search by service, then by proximity
Hours and services managed once, per clinic
Booking completable on a phone in under a minute
Accessibility treated as a requirement, not a review step

decisions.title: Service first, location second
decisions.body: A patient picks what they need, then sees which clinics offer it, how far each is and the next available slot at each.
decisions.why: It matches how patients actually decide, and it stopped the misdirected visits that were costing reception staff hours each week.

decisions.title: Clinic data entered once
decisions.body: Hours, services, clinicians and holiday closures live on one record per clinic and render everywhere that clinic appears.
decisions.why: The contradictions were not a design problem, they were a data problem. One record per clinic removed the whole class of error.

decisions.title: A booking flow built for one hand
decisions.body: Three steps, large targets, no account required, and a confirmation by SMS rather than email.
decisions.why: Most bookings happen on a phone, often one-handed and often in a hurry. The flow was built for that case rather than adapted to it.

designSystem.title: A system six clinics can share
designSystem.lead: Components built so a new location can launch without design work, and so accessibility holds without per-page review.

items.v: 16px minimum body, 4.5:1 contrast enforced in tokens
Clinic card, service card, slot picker, hours table
A seventh clinic is a content record, not a build

implementation.title: Static pages, live availability
implementation.lead: Clinic and service pages are statically rendered for speed; availability is fetched live from the practice-management system at the point of booking.
points: Clinic records drive pages, finder results and structured data
Live slot availability via the existing practice-management API
SMS confirmation and reminder on every booking
Local business structured data generated per clinic

projects.takeaway: Six sites were not six design problems. Consolidating clinic information into one record per location fixed the contradictions, and the booking flow could then be built once and trusted everywhere.

projects.headline: Qualified consultations up 3.3× from search
projects.statement: Building the practice-area pages a law firm needs to be found on, and the authority to rank them.

card.blurb: Practice-area pages written for the question a client actually types, not for the statute.
card.quote: The enquiries now arrive already in the right practice area.
card.cite: Sanjay Puri, Managing Partner @ Brij Legal

hero.label: Top-10 keywords by practice area
hero.caption: Ranking distribution across the firm’s seven practice areas.

challenge.title: Written for lawyers, found by nobody
challenge.lead: Brij’s practice-area pages were written in the language of the statute. Prospective clients search in the language of the problem, and the two almost never matched.
symptoms: Seven practice areas shared one page of about 200 words
No page addressed a question a non-lawyer would actually type
Partner profiles carried no practice context, so expertise was invisible to search
Referrals were the only meaningful source of new work

strategy.title: Write for the problem, not the statute
strategy.lead: Legal buyers search a situation before they search a service. The content plan started from those situations and connected each one to the practice area that handles it.

pillars.title: Search intent
pillars.body: We mapped the questions clients ask in a first call and treated each as a page, rather than starting from the firm’s own service taxonomy.

pillars.title: Practice-area architecture
pillars.body: Each of the seven areas got a full page with scope, typical engagements, the partners who handle it and an indicative fee structure.

pillars.title: Authority
pillars.body: Partner commentary placed in trade publications, each linking back to the relevant practice area rather than to the homepage.

pillars.title: Technical base
pillars.body: Fixed the JavaScript-rendered navigation that was leaving most of the site undiscovered, and added professional-service structured data.

keywords.query: how to exit a joint venture india

changes.title: Technical SEO
changes.body: Replaced the client-rendered navigation that had left 80% of pages undiscovered, and added structured data for the firm and its practitioners.

changes.title: On-page SEO
changes.body: Rebuilt seven practice-area pages and 23 partner profiles so each targets a defined set of queries.

changes.title: Content
changes.body: Published 41 situation-led guides, each written to answer one question completely and link to the practice area that handles it.

changes.title: Authority
changes.body: Placed partner commentary in eleven trade and business publications over the campaign, linking to practice areas rather than the homepage.

projects.growthNote: Search Console and the firm’s intake log, ten-month window against the ten months preceding it.

impact.title: A second pipeline next to the referral network
impact.lead: The referral network did not change. What changed is that the firm now has a second source of work it can actually influence.
points: Because the guides address a situation and the practice-area page sets out scope and fees, enquiries arrive pre-sorted — partners spend less of a first call establishing what the matter even is.
Three of the seven practice areas now generate enough search enquiries to justify their own associate, which was the firm’s stated objective.

projects.takeaway: Professional services rank by answering the question a client asks before they know what to call it. Rewriting from the problem rather than the statute was the whole campaign.

projects.headline: Organic bookings up 3.9× in seven months
projects.statement: Turning a tour operator’s itinerary pages into the destination research people actually search for.

card.blurb: Destination guides built where the demand already was, each feeding the itineraries that sell.
card.quote: We stopped bidding against aggregators for our own trips.

hero.label: Organic sessions by destination cluster
hero.caption: Sessions grouped by destination, over the campaign.

challenge.title: Competing with aggregators on their own terms
challenge.lead: Udaan’s site was a list of itineraries with prices. It competed directly with aggregators on booking queries, lost, and had nothing to offer the much larger research audience arriving earlier in the journey.
symptoms: Itinerary pages were the only content, and all of them targeted booking queries
No content addressed visa, season, cost or packing questions
Thin itinerary descriptions were duplicated across similar trips
Paid search was the only reliable source of bookings

strategy.title: Win the research, then route it
strategy.lead: Nobody books a trip on the first search. We built for the questions that come months earlier and connected each one to the itinerary it leads to.

pillars.title: Destination clusters
pillars.body: Each destination became a cluster: a guide, the practical questions, the seasonal advice, and the itineraries that serve it.

pillars.title: Research intent
pillars.body: Visa, best-season, budget and safety questions were treated as primary content rather than as blog filler.

pillars.title: Itinerary differentiation
pillars.body: Rewrote 60 itineraries so similar trips no longer competed with each other on near-identical copy.

pillars.title: Internal routing
pillars.body: Every guide ends with the itineraries it implies, so research traffic has a commercial next step.

changes.title: Technical SEO
changes.body: Consolidated the duplicate itinerary variants that were splitting authority, and fixed a canonical pattern that had seasonal pages competing with their own parents.

changes.title: Content
changes.body: Built eleven destination clusters, each with a guide, four to six practical questions and the itineraries that serve it.

changes.title: On-page SEO
changes.body: Rewrote 60 itinerary pages so each targets a distinct trip type rather than a shared destination keyword.

changes.title: Site structure
changes.body: Routed every guide into its matching itineraries, turning research sessions into a measurable booking path.

projects.growthNote: Search Console and the operator’s booking system, seven-month window, seasonally adjusted against the same months of the prior year.

impact.title: Reached earlier, at a lower cost
impact.lead: Meeting travellers at the research stage put Udaan in front of them months before an aggregator would have, and at no marginal cost per visit.
points: Research traffic converts more slowly than booking traffic but far more cheaply, which has let the operator reduce paid search on the destinations where the clusters are strongest.
The guides also give the sales team something to send during a long consideration period, which it did not previously have.

projects.takeaway: A tour operator cannot outbid an aggregator on booking queries, but it can out-answer one on the research that happens first. The clusters are what made that traffic worth having.

projects.headline: Site visits booked from search up 4.6×
projects.statement: Giving a residential developer a locality-led search presence instead of one page per project.

card.blurb: Locality pages that answer what buyers compare before they compare projects.
card.quote: Buyers arrive knowing the area, not just the brochure.
card.cite: Anjali Deshpande, Marketing Head @ Nilaya Homes

hero.label: Locality pages — ranking growth
hero.caption: Top-10 positions across the fourteen locality pages.

challenge.title: One page per project, nothing per locality
challenge.lead: Buyers search a locality long before they search a developer. Nilaya had a page for each of its nine projects and nothing at all for the fourteen localities those projects sit in.
symptoms: Portals outranked the developer on its own project names
Project pages went dark as soon as a project sold out, losing all accumulated authority
No locality, pricing or connectivity content of any kind
Google Business Profiles for the sales offices were unclaimed

strategy.title: Rank the locality, route to the project
strategy.lead: Locality pages outlive projects. Building them gave the site an asset that keeps its authority when a project completes and sells out.

pillars.title: Locality as the unit
pillars.body: Fourteen locality pages covering connectivity, pricing trends, schools, infrastructure and what is being built.

pillars.title: Projects as inventory
pillars.body: Project pages now hang off their locality, so a completed project redirects its authority rather than disappearing.

pillars.title: Local presence
pillars.body: Claimed and structured the sales-office profiles, with review generation tied to the site-visit flow.

pillars.title: Comparison content
pillars.body: Honest locality-versus-locality comparisons, including the ones where Nilaya does not build.

changes.title: Technical SEO
changes.body: Replaced the pattern that 404’d sold-out projects with redirects into their locality page, preserving nine years of accumulated links.

changes.title: Content
changes.body: Built fourteen locality pages and eleven comparison pages, each updated quarterly with current pricing data.

changes.title: Local SEO
changes.body: Claimed and structured four sales-office profiles, and tied review requests to the post-visit follow-up.

changes.title: Site structure
changes.body: Reorganised projects under localities so authority accumulates in the pages that persist.

projects.growthNote: Search Console, Business Profile insights and the developer’s CRM, nine-month window.

impact.title: An asset that survives the project cycle
impact.lead: The commercial point of locality pages is that they do not expire. A project sells out; the locality page keeps ranking and routes buyers to whatever is launching next.
points: Two new launches in month seven reached their first-month site-visit target without the paid campaign that previous launches had required.
Because locality pages carry honest comparisons, the buyers arriving at a site visit are better informed, which the sales team reports as shorter negotiations.

projects.takeaway: Project pages are inventory and inventory expires. Moving the SEO investment into locality pages gave the developer something that compounds across launches instead of resetting with each one.

projects.headline: Direct bookings up 2.9×, commission down
projects.statement: Winning back direct bookings for a boutique hotel group that had handed its search presence to the aggregators.

card.blurb: Property pages and local guides that beat the aggregators on the hotel’s own name and its neighbourhood.
card.quote: Every direct booking is a commission we keep.
card.cite: Ritu Malhotra, Commercial Director @ Serai Hotels

hero.label: Direct vs. aggregator share
hero.caption: Share of bookings by channel, over the campaign.

challenge.title: Outranked on its own name
challenge.lead: Aggregators occupied the first three results for every Serai property, including searches for the hotel by name. Each of those bookings cost the group 15–22% in commission.
symptoms: Property pages were thin and nearly identical across the three locations
No content about the surrounding area, which is most of what guests research
Booking engine on a separate subdomain with no internal linking
Reviews scattered across platforms, none structured for search

strategy.title: Be the best page about your own hotel
strategy.lead: Aggregators have authority but generic content. The one thing they cannot do is know the property and its neighbourhood better than the people who run it.

pillars.title: Property depth
pillars.body: Every room type, rate, policy and facility documented properly — more detail than any aggregator listing carries.

pillars.title: Neighbourhood guides
pillars.body: What to do within walking distance, written by the staff who actually live there.

pillars.title: Booking continuity
pillars.body: Moved the booking engine onto the main domain so the path from search to booking stays on one site.

pillars.title: Structured reviews
pillars.body: Consolidated and marked up reviews so ratings surface in the result itself.

keywords.query: things to do near jaipur old city

changes.title: Technical SEO
changes.body: Migrated the booking engine onto the main domain, consolidating authority that had been split across two hostnames for four years.

changes.title: On-page SEO
changes.body: Rebuilt three property pages and nineteen room-type pages, each with full rates, policies and facilities.

changes.title: Content
changes.body: Published 27 neighbourhood guides written by property staff, each linking to the property it surrounds.

changes.title: Local SEO
changes.body: Consolidated review signals and added hotel structured data so ratings and prices appear in the result.

projects.growthNote: Search Console and the group’s property-management system, eleven-month window, compared like-for-like by season.

impact.title: The same room night, a larger share of it
impact.lead: Shifting bookings from aggregator to direct does not add guests. It changes what each guest is worth.
points: Direct share moved from 21% to 49% of bookings, and every point of that shift is commission the group keeps.
Direct guests also book longer stays on average, which the group attributes to the neighbourhood guides setting up a longer itinerary before arrival.

projects.takeaway: An aggregator will always have more authority. It will never have better information about the property, and on a brand or neighbourhood query that turned out to be the deciding factor.

projects.headline: Cost per qualified lead down 56%
projects.statement: Rebuilding a modular-kitchen brand’s paid acquisition around measured showroom visits instead of form fills.

card.blurb: A qualifying question in the ad itself, so the expensive leads never enter the funnel.
card.quote: Half the leads, twice the showroom visits.

hero.label: Cost per qualified lead — monthly
hero.caption: Cost measured against leads that reached a showroom visit.

challenge.title: Cheap leads that never became customers
challenge.lead: Zafran was generating leads at a low cost and converting almost none. A modular kitchen is a six-figure purchase and most of the enquiries had no budget anywhere near it.
symptoms: Lead forms asked nothing that would indicate budget or timeline
The sales team called every lead, which absorbed most of its week
Campaigns optimised for lead volume, which actively selected for unqualified leads
No measurement connected an ad to a showroom visit

campaign.title: Make the ad do the qualifying
campaign.lead: The cheapest way to reduce the cost of a qualified lead is to stop paying for unqualified ones. Most of the work was moving qualification earlier.
campaign.audience: Homeowners in possession or near-possession, within 12km of a showroom
campaign.offer: Free 3D design consultation with an indicative price band stated up front
campaign.creative: Real installed kitchens with the price band on the creative itself

funnel.body: Price band shown on the creative, so people who are not in that range self-select out.
Three qualifying questions — possession status, kitchen size, budget band — before any contact field.
Qualified visitors book a showroom slot directly; others get a design guide instead.
Showroom attendance imported back as an offline conversion, so the platforms optimise for visits.

execution.title: Campaign structure
execution.body: One campaign per showroom with its own radius, replacing a single national campaign that advertised showrooms 400km from the viewer.

execution.title: Creative
execution.body: Photographs of actual installed kitchens with the honest starting price on the image, which cut click volume and raised click quality.

execution.title: Landing pages
execution.body: Qualification moved ahead of the contact fields, so an unqualified visitor never becomes a lead in the first place.

execution.title: Measurement
execution.body: Showroom attendance imported weekly as an offline conversion, giving the platforms the real objective to bid against.

optimisations.decision: Put the price band on the creative
optimisations.reason: A third of leads were disqualified on budget during the first call.
optimisations.outcome: Click volume fell by about 40%; qualified lead volume rose.

optimisations.decision: Switched the optimisation event to showroom visit
optimisations.reason: Lead-optimised campaigns were systematically finding the cheapest, least qualified audience.
optimisations.outcome: Cost per lead rose, cost per qualified lead fell by more than half.

optimisations.decision: Added possession status as the first question
optimisations.reason: Buyers more than six months from possession almost never converted inside the campaign window.
optimisations.outcome: They now receive a guide and a follow-up sequence instead of a sales call.

optimisations.decision: Cut the radius from 25km to 12km
optimisations.reason: Showroom attendance fell off sharply beyond 12km regardless of lead quality.
optimisations.outcome: Same budget, materially higher attendance rate.

projects.beforeAfterNote: Month six against month zero. Cost per lead rising is the intended effect, not a regression — the qualified figure is the one the business manages against.

businessResult.title: Fewer leads, more kitchens
businessResult.lead: This campaign deliberately made the headline metric look worse. Cost per lead more than doubled, and that is the point.
points: The sales team now calls roughly half as many leads and books nearly three times the showroom visits, which freed up most of a week per consultant.
Because budget bands are stated before the first conversation, the design consultation starts from a realistic brief rather than a correction.

projects.takeaway: Optimising for lead volume on a high-consideration purchase buys the wrong audience very efficiently. Moving qualification into the ad cost half the clicks and more than doubled the showroom traffic.

projects.headline: Repeat-purchase revenue up 3.1×
projects.statement: Shifting a skincare brand’s paid spend from first orders to the second one, where the margin actually is.

card.blurb: Acquisition judged on 90-day value rather than on the first order, which changed every budget decision.
card.quote: We were buying customers who never came back.

hero.label: 90-day customer value by cohort
hero.caption: Revenue per acquired customer over 90 days, by acquisition month.

challenge.title: Profitable on paper, unprofitable in practice
challenge.lead: Mira’s campaigns reported a healthy ROAS on first orders. The business was not growing, because a heavy first-order discount was buying customers who never returned.
symptoms: A 30% first-order discount carried in almost every ad
Reported ROAS counted the discounted first order and nothing after it
Repeat-purchase rate at 90 days was under 12%
The highest-margin products were never advertised

campaign.title: Buy the customer, not the order
campaign.lead: We changed the number the campaigns were judged on from first-order ROAS to 90-day customer value, and let the budget follow.
campaign.audience: Routine-building buyers segmented by concern, with separate creative for first purchase and replenishment
campaign.offer: Discount replaced with a trial set and a replenishment reminder
campaign.creative: Results-over-time sequences and a routine explainer, refreshed every three weeks

funnel.body: Concern-matched creative leading to a routine rather than a single product.
A routine builder that assembles two or three products for the stated concern.
Trial set purchased, with replenishment timing set at checkout.
Cohort tracked for 90 days, and that figure — not the first order — drives budget.

execution.title: Campaign structure
execution.body: Separated first-purchase and replenishment campaigns so the two stopped competing for the same customer at the same price.

execution.title: Creative
execution.body: Replaced discount-led creative with results-over-time sequences, which carried a lower click-through rate and a much higher repeat rate.

execution.title: Landing pages
execution.body: A routine builder in place of single product pages, raising first-order value and setting up a natural replenishment date.

execution.title: Measurement
execution.body: Cohort reporting at 30, 60 and 90 days, replacing single-session ROAS as the decision metric.

optimisations.decision: Retired the 30% first-order discount
optimisations.reason: Discount-acquired cohorts repeated at under a third the rate of full-price ones.
optimisations.outcome: First-order volume fell; 90-day cohort value rose well past the shortfall.

optimisations.decision: Moved budget to the routine builder
optimisations.reason: Multi-product first orders repeated at roughly twice the rate of single-product ones.
optimisations.outcome: Higher first-order value and a higher repeat rate from the same spend.

optimisations.decision: Built a replenishment campaign timed to product life
optimisations.reason: Repeat purchases clustered at 45–60 days with no prompt in place.
optimisations.outcome: Second-order rate improved materially at a low cost per order.

optimisations.decision: Judged every campaign on 90-day value
optimisations.reason: First-order ROAS was systematically favouring the least valuable customers.
optimisations.outcome: Budget moved away from two campaigns that had looked like the best performers.

projects.beforeAfterNote: Month five cohort against month zero cohort, each measured over a full 90 days. First-order ROAS falling is the intended trade.

businessResult.title: A worse-looking ROAS and a better business
businessResult.lead: First-order ROAS dropped by about a third. Over 90 days the same spend now returns roughly three times the revenue.
points: Because customers arrive on a routine rather than on a discount, repeat revenue is predictable enough for the brand to plan production against it.
The highest-margin products, previously never advertised, now enter through the routine builder rather than needing their own campaign.

projects.takeaway: Single-session ROAS is the wrong metric for a repeat-purchase category. Changing it to 90-day cohort value made the first-order numbers look worse and the business considerably stronger.

projects.headline: Cost per approved application down 44%
projects.statement: Moving a lending brand’s paid acquisition from applications started to applications actually approved.

card.blurb: Eligibility moved into the ad, so the campaigns stopped buying applications that were always going to be declined.
card.quote: Approval rate was a marketing problem all along.
card.cite: Deepak Menon, Growth Head @ Arka Finserv

hero.label: Applications started vs. approved
hero.caption: Monthly applications by stage, over the campaign.

challenge.title: Paying for applications that were always going to fail
challenge.lead: Arka was acquiring applications at a competitive cost and approving fewer than one in five. The campaigns had no visibility of approval, so they optimised for the audience most likely to start an application and least likely to pass underwriting.
symptoms: Approval rate at 18%, with no approval signal reaching either platform
Eligibility criteria appeared only after six form steps
One campaign covered four loan products with very different criteria
Applicants who were declined received no alternative, so the acquisition cost was wasted entirely

campaign.title: Advertise the criteria, not just the rate
campaign.lead: Stating eligibility in the ad costs clicks and saves applications. We then fed approvals back so the platforms could find the audience that passes.
campaign.audience: Salaried applicants matching each product’s income and credit criteria, segmented by product
campaign.offer: Indicative rate with eligibility stated up front and a sixty-second eligibility check
campaign.creative: Plain-language criteria and a worked repayment example

funnel.body: Minimum income and credit criteria stated in the ad copy itself.
A sixty-second eligibility check before any document upload or personal detail.
Eligible applicants continue; ineligible ones are routed to a product that fits or to guidance.
Approval imported back as an offline conversion, so bidding targets approved applicants.

execution.title: Campaign structure
execution.body: Split one campaign into four, one per loan product, each with its own criteria in the copy and its own eligibility check.

execution.title: Creative
execution.body: Replaced rate-led headlines with criteria-led ones and a worked repayment example, which reduced clicks and raised approval rate.

execution.title: Landing pages
execution.body: A sixty-second eligibility check placed ahead of document upload, so ineligible applicants never reach a step that costs the business money.

execution.title: Measurement
execution.body: Approval and disbursal imported daily from underwriting as offline conversions.

optimisations.decision: Put minimum income in the ad copy
optimisations.reason: Just over half of declines were on income criteria that were never stated before the application.
optimisations.outcome: Click volume fell; approval rate rose within the first month.

optimisations.decision: Optimised for approval rather than application start
optimisations.reason: Platforms were finding high-intent, low-eligibility applicants very efficiently.
optimisations.outcome: Cost per application rose, cost per approved application fell by 44%.

optimisations.decision: Routed declined applicants to a product that fits
optimisations.reason: A declined applicant had already been paid for and was being discarded.
optimisations.outcome: A measurable share now convert on a secured product instead.

optimisations.decision: Paused the broadest keyword set
optimisations.reason: Generic loan queries converted at a fifth the approval rate of product-specific ones.
optimisations.outcome: Budget moved to product-specific queries at a better approved cost.

projects.beforeAfterNote: Month seven against month zero, using underwriting records for both periods.

businessResult.title: Twice the approved book on a similar budget
businessResult.lead: Monthly spend rose modestly while approved applications roughly doubled, because the campaigns stopped paying for people who could never be approved.
points: Underwriting workload per approval fell sharply, since far fewer applications now reach manual review only to be declined.
Stating criteria in the ad also reduced complaints about the application experience, which had been a recurring compliance concern.

projects.takeaway: In lending, the conversion that matters sits inside underwriting rather than inside the ad platform. Feeding approvals back and stating criteria up front changed which audience the campaigns went looking for.

projects.headline: ROAS from 1.9× to 5.2× across two seasons
projects.statement: Building a seasonal paid acquisition plan for a toy brand whose entire year turns on eleven weeks.

card.blurb: Audiences built in the quiet months so the peak season had something to scale into.
card.quote: We stopped starting from zero every October.

hero.label: Spend and ROAS by week
hero.caption: Weekly spend against return, across the build-up and the peak.

challenge.title: Eleven weeks of revenue, twelve months of cost
challenge.lead: Patang made most of its year in the festive and gifting weeks, and spent those weeks acquiring cold audiences at the most expensive moment of the year. Campaigns were switched off in the quiet months, so every season started from nothing.
symptoms: Spend concentrated entirely in the eleven highest-cost weeks of the year
No retargeting pool at the start of each season, so everything was prospecting
Creative produced in-season under time pressure
Stock planning disconnected from what the campaigns were pushing

campaign.title: Spend in the quiet months, harvest in the loud ones
campaign.lead: The plan moved a deliberate share of the budget into the off-season to build an audience the peak campaigns could retarget rather than discover.
campaign.audience: Parents and gift-buyers by child age band, built in the off-season and harvested in peak
campaign.offer: Age-matched gift guides off-season; bundles and delivery guarantees in peak
campaign.creative: Play-pattern video shot in advance, tested off-season at low cost

funnel.body: Off-season: age-band gift guides at a low cost per engaged visitor. Peak: bundles to the pool already built.
An age-filtered guide off-season; a bundle page with a delivery-by date in peak.
Off-season visitors join a segment by child age band; peak visitors buy.
Purchase matched back to acquisition season, so off-season spend is credited properly.

execution.title: Campaign structure
execution.body: A year-round build campaign at a modest budget, plus a peak campaign that spends almost entirely against the audience the build campaign created.

execution.title: Creative
execution.body: Play-pattern video shot and tested in the quiet months, so peak-season creative was already proven when it mattered.

execution.title: Landing pages
execution.body: Age-band gift guides year-round; bundle pages with a delivery-by date during the peak weeks.

execution.title: Measurement
execution.body: Purchases attributed back to the season in which the customer was acquired, so off-season spend is not judged on same-week revenue.

optimisations.decision: Moved roughly a fifth of annual budget into the off-season
optimisations.reason: Cost per engaged visitor off-season was a fraction of the peak-week figure.
optimisations.outcome: Peak season opened with a large warm pool instead of none.

optimisations.decision: Tested all peak creative off-season
optimisations.reason: In-season testing wastes the most expensive impressions on learning.
optimisations.outcome: Peak campaigns launched with proven creative and no learning phase.

optimisations.decision: Segmented by child age band rather than by product
optimisations.reason: Gift-buyers shop by age, not by category.
optimisations.outcome: Higher click-through rate and a much better match between ad and landing page.

optimisations.decision: Capped spend on out-of-stock lines
optimisations.reason: A meaningful share of peak spend had been driving traffic to unavailable products.
optimisations.outcome: Budget redirected to in-stock lines within the same week.

beforeAfter.metric: Share of peak spend to warm audiences

projects.beforeAfterNote: This season’s peak eleven weeks against the same eleven weeks of the prior year.

businessResult.title: A season that compounds instead of restarting
businessResult.lead: The off-season budget is not a cost against the quiet months. It is the thing that makes the peak weeks affordable.
points: Peak revenue more than tripled on a roughly similar total annual spend, because the expensive weeks were spent harvesting rather than prospecting.
Connecting campaign budget to stock availability removed a recurring waste that had gone unnoticed in previous seasons.

projects.takeaway: A seasonal business cannot afford to meet its customers for the first time during its most expensive weeks. Moving a fifth of the budget forward was what made the peak weeks profitable.
